rows.reviewerNote: Lines 5-8: the key (coat and horse colour) is the only thing ascertained from the window. Ten minutes (line 4), cheerful (36-37), ten thousand (29, Darcy's) and liking the house (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at lines 36 and 37, at the ball — true, and a different part of the passage. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.
changes.after: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at the ball, at lines 36 and 37: true of him, but from a later part of the passage. From the upper window at lines 7 and 8 the daughters learned only that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

changes.before: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.
changes.after: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. From the upper window at lines 7 and 8 the daughters learned only that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 23-24: an oak torn up by the roots falls across the road. Branch (John's worry, line 20), bridge (47) and leaves (4-5) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True of line 4, at the start of the journey, not here. In the window, line 22 answers the stem: 'The words were scarcely out of his mouth when'.
changes.after: The dry leaves blown across the road are at lines 4 and 5, at the start of the journey, outside lines 22 to 24. Within the window, lines 23 and 24 give what fell: an oak, torn up by the roots.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 14-15: fear of his flying about and never settled at Netherfield. Cooked dinner (unstated), Lady Lucas's idea (16-17), twelve ladies (18) and dislike (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: The twelve ladies are line 18, and it is the GIRLS who grieve over them at line 18, not Mrs Bennet. In the window, line 14 answers the stem: 'his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear'.
changes.after: The twelve ladies are at line 18, outside lines 13 to 16, and it is the girls who grieve over them there, not Mrs Bennet. Her fear is at lines 14 and 15: that he might always be flying about and never settled at Netherfield.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 50: 'It is said' (and 'If he did', line 51) puts the report at second hand. Sympathy (unstated), not daring (24, about laughing) and penitence (51, what he did next) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at line 24, outside this window; that was about laughing, not about this. In the window, line 50 answers the stem: 'It is said—I won’t vouch for the fact—that Captain'.
changes.after: The narrator did not dare at line 24, outside this window, and that was about laughing at the reading, not about this report. Line 50 gives her reason: 'It is said', so she has the story only from others.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 11: obliged to be in town (London, line 16) the following day. Lady Lucas, motive, courses (9-10, Mrs Bennet's) and London party (15-17) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. In the window, line 11 answers the stem: 'which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to'.
changes.after: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. His answer, at line 11, says only that he was obliged to be in town the following day.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 5-6: hopes of a sight of the young ladies. Book (unstated), invitation reversed (lines 9-12, the Bennets'), horse (line 8, Bingley's own) and dance (60-61, later) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: The black horse at line 8 is a thing the ladies saw, turned into something he wanted. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.
changes.after: The black horse at line 8 is the one Mr Bingley himself rode, carried across to Mr Bennet and turned into something Mr Bingley wanted. Lines 5 and 6 give what he hoped for: a sight of the young ladies.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 31-32: his manners, proud and above his company. Not rich (33 still a large estate), looks (34-35 the result, not the cause), Bingley's complaint (37-38) and 'from the moment he walked in' (30-31 admired half the evening) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 31 answers the stem: 'with great admiration for about half the evening, till'.
changes.after: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. Lines 31 and 32 give what changed the room: his manners, as he was found to be proud and above his company.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 50: no extra charge to sit by him; the fare is already paid at line 16. Bundle and lilacs (14), the front seat (51, what she gets) and reins (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at line 14, outside this window; those went in before they set off. In the window, line 50 answers the stem: '"You can come up if you want to; there'.
changes.after: The bundle and the lilacs are at line 14, outside this window, put in beside her by her mother before the coach set off; they are not a cost. At line 50 Mr Cobb says there is no extra charge to sit by him.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 1: 'Go and fetch my fishing-rod'. Watching (line 3, Mark's offer), going round (30-31, Mark's own act) and keeping quiet (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at lines 30 and 31, a long way outside this window. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: '“Go and fetch my fishing-rod,” whispered Bevis, unable to'.
changes.after: Going round the cliff to get in front is what Mark does at lines 30 and 31, a long way outside this window, and Bevis never asks for it. At line 1 Bevis asks Mark to fetch his fishing-rod.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 3-6: whether the thief has anywhere to go ('No country is safe' / 'The world is big enough'). Shrewd fellow (1-2), the world shrinking (from line 10) and England (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at lines 10 and 11, four lines past the end of this window. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: '“I maintain,” said Stuart, “that the chances are in'.
changes.after: Stuart and Ralph do argue about whether the world has grown smaller, but that starts at line 10, four lines past the end of this window. Within lines 3 to 6 they disagree about where the thief can go: Ralph says at line 3 that no country is safe for him.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 45-46: Fogg's twenty thousand deposited at Baring's. Least possible time (50-51, the objector's), four thousand (42, Stuart's) and everything he owns (74, half his fortune) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at line 42, three lines before this window. In the window, line 45 answers the stem: '“All right,” said Mr. Fogg; and, turning to the'.
changes.after: Stuart wagers four thousand at line 42, three lines before this window opens at line 45, and the child gives Stuart's stake as Fogg's. Fogg's own stake, at lines 45 and 46, is the twenty thousand he has deposited at Baring's.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 31 and 33: netting against two jumpers. Date (32), post (6) and width (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: A post is at line 6, far above this window. In the window, line 31 answers the stem: 'Their end has proper netting'.
changes.after: A post is mentioned at line 6, far above this window, where the ball 'goes by the post' and Kieran swears it was in. It is not a difference between the ends: line 31 gives their end proper netting, and line 33 gives ours two jumpers.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 5-6: scratch himself anywhere he pleased with any leg. Tail (6, not a leg), lap (32) and running faster (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at line 32, where he goes up to watch the writing. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'He could scratch himself anywhere he pleased with any'.
changes.after: Climbing up into the big man's lap is at line 32, outside this window, where he goes up to watch the writing. Lines 5 and 6 give what he could do with any leg he chose: scratch himself anywhere he pleased.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 13: curled in on themselves and gone crisp. Soak (14, what he did), going over in the wind (7-8, dahlias) and the open door (unstated) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: Line 7 says that of Denise’s dahlias, and these are tomato leaves. In the window, line 13 answers the stem: 'Inside the greenhouse the tomato leaves had curled in'.
changes.after: Going over in the wind is said of Denise's dahlias at lines 7 and 8, outside this window, and these are tomato leaves. Line 13 gives what happened to the tomato leaves: they had curled in on themselves and gone crisp.

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 35-36: got through half and passed me the rest. Enormous breakfast (36, what he said), counting (23, potatoes) and keeping them back (unstated; 35 gives one o'clock) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: True at line 23, and it is the potatoes. In the window, line 35 answers the stem: 'We had the sandwiches on the crate at one'.
changes.after: Counting out loud into the bucket is at line 23, outside this window, and it is the potatoes Grandad counts, not the sandwiches. Lines 35 and 36 give what he did with his sandwich: he got through half and passed the narrator the rest.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 51: 'I must have you dance.' Stem quote is exact at lines 51-52. Rudeness (55-56, Darcy's reply), going home and pity for ladies all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: The rudeness about the ladies is lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. In the window, line 51 answers the stem: '“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance'.
changes.after: The rudeness about the ladies is at lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. Mr Bingley's aim is at line 51: 'I must have you dance.'

rows.reviewerNote: Lines 21-22: 'party' is the five who entered together. Dominant sense, political sense, the Netherfield ball (38) and everyone at the assembly (wrong value) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: The Netherfield ball is line 38, at the very end of the evening — a true event from a different part. In the window, line 21 answers the stem: 'cousin. And when the party entered the assembly-room, it'.
changes.after: Mr Bingley talks of giving a ball at Netherfield at line 38, later in the passage, and the child carries that party-like event back to line 21. At line 21 'party' is the group that entered the assembly-room, counted at lines 21 and 22 as five people.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 38: he takes the rule and re-measures, so it is a measuring tool. Law (dominant sense), mark on the wall (34-35) and 'as a rule' (neighbouring sense) all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: Reuses the mark on the wall from line 34; the rule is a separate thing he takes up. In the window, line 38 answers the stem: 'down. And he would take the rule, and re-measure'.
changes.after: The child reuses the mark he made on the wall at lines 34 and 35, but the rule is a separate thing he takes up. At line 38 he takes the rule and re-measures with it, so it is a measuring tool, not a line on the wall.

rows.reviewerNote: Line 1: woke Phyllis by pulling her hair gently. Shouting (line 4, after she stirs), blankets (unstated) and the reversal all fail. Executions are true.

changes.before: Roberta does shout, at line 4, and that is after Phyllis has begun to stir. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: 'Next morning Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair'.
changes.after: Roberta does call out 'Wake up! wake up!' at line 4, outside this window, after Phyllis has already stirred and answered at line 3. Line 1 gives how she woke her: by pulling her hair gently.
